cards.fact: He worked out the size of the Earth from one hilltop in the Punjab: first the hill's height, then how far the horizon dipped below level from its top. His answer was within about one percent of today's.
cards.art: Al-Biruni about 1020 on the flat rocky top of a hill near the fort of Nandana in the Punjab, early morning, explaining to a young student how the size of the Earth can be worked out from the hill: a lean Persian scholar of about fifty with a short graying beard and a plain white turban, in a long dark coat, kneeling on the rock behind a flat-topped boulder that comes up to his chest. On the boulder lies a wooden dust board, a flat tray spread with fine pale sand, and with a pointed wooden stick in his right hand he has drawn in the sand one simple geometric figure of lines only, his method: a large circle for the Earth; standing up on the top of the circle a small triangular hill, its peak clearly above the circle; a long straight line running from the hill's peak down to the right, staying OUTSIDE the circle, just grazing the circle's edge at one point on its upper right and going on past it (the line of sight to the horizon), never entering the circle; and two straight lines from the circle's center, one up through the hill to its peak and one out to the point where the grazing line touches the circle, so the three lines make a long thin triangle. No line crosses the circle from side to side. His left arm is held out level, his open hand pointing across to the far horizon. Beside the board on the boulder lies his brass astrolabe, a flat round disk about as wide as his hand is long, with its ring and a thin sighting rule across its face, lying flat and not being used. One young student, about sixteen, in a plain coloured coat and a small cap, kneels at the boulder's other side and looks where his teacher is pointing. Behind and below them the hill falls away steeply to a wide, flat, hazy plain of dry fields and villages, plainly land and not sea, whose edge meets the sky in a long level horizon line. Seen from low, beside the boulder, so that the dust board with its drawing, Al-Biruni's face and his pointing hand are all in the upper half of the picture, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Only two people. No one holds anything up to his eye. No letters, numbers or writing in the sand or anywhere: the drawing is lines only. No telescope, no glass lenses, no globe, no modern compass, no paper book. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The figure for the radius varies between sources (6,339.6 or 6,339.9 km against a mean of about 6,371 km); 'within about one percent' holds for both. His treatise on the astrolabe is listed among his works but its title was not returned.

cards.fact: The king of Denmark gave him a whole island, where he measured the planets night after night without a telescope, more exactly than anyone before him. He wore a nose of brass after losing his own in a duel.
cards.art: Tycho Brahe about 1585 at night in his observatory of Uraniborg on the island of Hven, standing in front of his great wall quadrant: a stout Danish nobleman of about forty, seen from the waist up and large in the picture at the right, his round face turned three-quarters toward us, a high balding forehead with short reddish hair, a broad reddish mustache curling out to the sides and a short pointed beard. Over the upper bridge of his nose, from between his eyebrows halfway down the nose, he wears a small fitted piece of polished brass shaped like the bridge of a nose, its edges lying close on his skin, plainly a separate metal piece; below it the lower half of his own nose, its tip and nostrils, is ordinary skin. The brass bridge catches the candlelight and is the brightest spot on his face. He wears a black doublet with a white ruff and a gold chain, and raises one hand to give a signal. Behind him at the left, fixed flat against a plain white plastered wall, the quadrant: a large flat brass instrument shaped exactly like a slice of pie that is one quarter of a circle, like the lower-left quarter of a clock face, from 6 o'clock to 9 o'clock. The center of that clock face is a small square opening in the wall, high up, just to the left of Tycho's head, showing the night sky and one bright planet. From the opening one straight brass bar runs level to the left (the 9 o'clock line) and a second straight brass bar of the same length runs straight down (the 6 o'clock line); a curved brass arc engraved with fine degree marks joins the far ends of the two bars, bulging out toward the lower left. The two straight bars meet only at the opening, in a right angle; the curved arc never touches the opening. The instrument is a little taller than a man (each bar about two metres). At the lower left a young assistant in a plain coat, smaller with distance, stands by the curved arc holding up a candle lantern to read the degree marks, his face a hand's width from the arc. Nobody puts an eye to any instrument. Seen from across the room, Tycho's head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with plain wall above it. A plastered room with a ceiling. Two people only. No telescope anywhere (it had not been invented), no lenses, no globe, no drawn lines of sight. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: The armies of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore fired rockets with iron cases that could fly a kilometer or more. Captured ones were taken to Britain, where William Congreve studied them and built his own.
cards.art: A Mysore rocket being launched in 1780, in Hyder Ali's army at Pollilur. Seen from low and to one side, the whole rocket and its frame stand in the middle of the picture, well away from both top corners. The rocket: a small black iron tube only as long as a man's forearm and only as thick as his wrist, with a short pointed iron nose, lashed with cord to the front end of one long straight bamboo pole about four times as long as the tube. There is only one bamboo pole, and the tube is at its very front: nothing sticks out past the tube's nose. The rocket rests on a separate light launching frame of two thin wooden sticks crossed and tied together near their tops like a tall X, standing on the ground; the bamboo pole simply lies loose in the open fork above the tie, resting there and not tied to the frame, so it can fly free, with the iron tube just past the fork, and the rest of the pole slopes down behind the frame until its back end rests on the ground. The rocket points up and away to the right at a moderate angle, about forty degrees above the ground, so that its iron nose is two thirds of the way across the picture and a third of the way down, with plain sky all around it and above it. The fuse is one short cord that hangs down from the back end of the iron tube, just behind the cord lashing; there is no other cord, rod or fuse anywhere on the bamboo pole. The bamboo pole is long: from the iron tube it runs down past the fork of the frame and on behind it, all the way to the ground, where its back end rests in the dirt, much longer than the frame is tall. A rocketman of Hyder Ali's army, a lean man of about thirty, stands beside the frame on the left and reaches out to the fuse, touching the lower end of that hanging fuse, just under the iron tube, with a smoldering slow match, a glowing cord held in a short wooden holder. He is dressed as Hyder Ali's soldiers of 1780 were: a plain white cotton turban, a knee-length coat of dark green broadcloth closed at the side and tied with a cream cotton sash at the waist, loose cream drawers to the calf, bare feet; no stripes or animal patterns on any clothing. His head is two fifths of the way down the picture and a third of the way across. One older officer in a large white turban and a long dark coat with a sash stands farther back holding a short staff at his side, watching. A second rocket of the same kind, small and far off, already rises in an arc with its bamboo pole trailing behind it and one trail of white smoke. Behind, the dusty red plain and a fort's walls far off. Two people only. No one raises a hand or holds anything up to the eye: no telescope, no spyglass. No tiger stripes, no modern rockets, no fins, no European uniforms, no second bamboo pole. H4 is one round silver case like a very large pocket watch, about 13 centimetres across: a little wider than his palm and no bigger than his face (his hand is about as long as his face). It lies face up in his palm, tilted toward us: a white enamel dial with small black Roman hour marks round its edge, a ring of fine minute marks, two ornate dark hands, and a small black painted flower-and-leaf scroll pattern around the center, a small silver ring at the top of the case; one single dial with no small extra dials, no compass star and no compass needle; no lid stands open and no works show. cards.fact: Navigators of the Marshall Islands tied palm ribs and shells into charts of how ocean swells bend around islands. They learned them by heart on land, and at sea they steered by feeling the swells under the canoe.
cards.art: A Marshallese stick chart about 1860, shown by a navigator on the beach. The chart is a light, open frame of thin palm-leaf midribs lashed together with coconut fiber, about as long as a man's arm, made of only about a dozen sticks, and it is lopsided and irregular like a real Marshallese rebbelib in a museum: not a rectangle, not a grid, not a star and not a web. One long straight stick runs across it on a slant; a second straight stick crosses it at a sharp, uneven angle near one end; on the left side two curved sticks bow outward in arcs of different sizes, and on the right side one long gentle curve sweeps around, like ocean swells bending around islands; three short sticks stick out at odd slants beyond the others, and the outline of the whole chart is ragged and uneven, with no straight border. Most of the chart is open space between the sticks. The sticks are lashed with fiber where they cross, and small white cowrie shells are tied on at four scattered places, unevenly spaced, to mark islands. The navigator, an older Marshallese man with a lined face, short gray hair and a fringed fiber skirt, stands on the beach and holds the chart out in front of his chest in both hands, flat and tilted toward us, at the height of his breastbone; a young man of about seventeen stands close beside him, leaning in, and both look down at it. Both faces are well above the chart: no stick is in front of any face. Behind them, the lagoon, palms and an outrigger canoe with a triangular sail. Seen from in front, a little below their chests, the two heads a fifth of the way down the picture with plain sky above them, the older man's head three fifths of the way across, and the whole chart just below their faces, between a third and a half of the way down the picture, a fifth of the picture's width in from each side. Only two people. One chart, lashed where its sticks cross; no compass, no paper map, no feather headdresses. cards.art: The transit of Venus on 3 June 1769 at Point Venus on Tahiti, in broad morning daylight: Charles Green, the astronomer of Cook's party, an Englishman of about thirty-five in shirtsleeves and a wide straw hat, sits on a stool behind a Gregorian reflecting telescope by James Short and looks into it. The telescope must be drawn as a Gregorian reflector, not a refractor: a polished brass tube about as long as his arm from shoulder to wrist and about four times as long as it is wide (not a fat drum, not a long thin pipe), with an open front end and a closed back end with a round end plate; the small eyepiece sticks straight out of the CENTER of that back end plate, on the line of the tube, with a small dark glass fitted over it; a thin brass focusing rod runs along the outside of the tube from the back end to the front, and a small finder tube is clamped on top. The tube sits on a short brass pillar with three curved claw feet, which stands on a small square wooden table in front of him. Green sits at the left of the picture facing right; the telescope stands in the middle; the Sun is up and to the right of the telescope, and the telescope is aimed exactly at it: the tube is tilted up at about fifty degrees, its open front end pointing straight at the Sun, so that the line of the tube, carried on, runs into the middle of the Sun. His eye is pressed to the dark glass of the eyepiece at the back end, on the line of the tube, one eye shut; he looks INTO the eyepiece, not past it and not at the sky, and his face is close behind the back of the tube. No eyepiece at the side, no lens at the front end. The sky is a pale cream haze with streaks of orange, not night and not a dark blue sky. The Sun is a solid, filled, flat disk of bright pale cream, plainly lighter and brighter than the hazy sky around it (not an outline, not a ring with the sky showing through), with a thin orange rim, about a fifth of the picture's width across, its center three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down: there is open sky above the Sun at least as tall as the Sun, and the Sun is well away from the right edge and from both top corners. One small black round dot, Venus, about a twenty-fifth of the Sun's width, sits just inside the Sun's lower left edge. At the right of the picture, behind the telescope, a second man, older, in a plain coat, stands at the open flap of a canvas tent with a notebook, counting the seconds from a tall wooden-cased pendulum clock standing inside the tent, its face plain with tick marks only, no numerals. Behind them a low earth bank topped with a wooden fence, the black-sand beach, palm trees and the masts of the Endeavour in the bay. Seen from low, beside and a little behind the observer, the Sun with its dot, the telescope and Green's head all in the upper half of the picture, his head two fifths of the way across the picture and a third of the way down. Only two people. No one looks at the Sun without the dark glass. No modern equipment. cards.art: Synesius of Cyrene about 400 in his country house near Cyrene, writing a letter: a lean, dark-haired Greek of Libya of about thirty with a short beard, in a plain pale tunic and a dark cloak, sitting at a small wooden table under a window and writing on a sheet of papyrus with a reed pen, and beside the papyrus lies an open wax tablet with a simple sketch scratched on it of the instrument he is asking for: a slender upright tube with notches down its side and a weighted cone at its foot. Through the window, dry hills, an olive tree and a hunting dog asleep in the sun. Seen from the side of the table, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, the papyrus and the wax tablet with its sketch in the upper half. Only him. The writing is small marks that cannot be read. No bishop's robes, no crosses, no printed books, no finished instrument on the table, no glass instruments. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. cards.check: Checked by a web search on 2026-11-13 (the Catholic Encyclopedia, New Advent): he studied under Hypatia at Alexandria and wrote her several letters that survive; his last called her 'a mother, a sister and a teacher'; envoy of Cyrene to Arcadius at Constantinople (397 or 398 to 400 or 402), where he gave his speech On Kingship and asked for tax relief; bishop of Ptolemais in 409 or 410; his letter to Hypatia asking for a hydroscope of brass (Letter 15) is the earliest known mention of a hydrometer. cards.fact: A Boston silversmith, he rode with the news for the town's patriot committees. On the night of 18 April 1775 he rode to Lexington to warn that British troops were on the march. He was caught on the road to Concord, but Samuel Prescott got through.
cards.art: Paul Revere on the night of 18 April 1775 riding through the countryside outside Boston: a solid, broad-faced man of forty, a recognizable likeness from Copley's portrait of him (a round, strong face, dark eyes under heavy dark brows, a firm chin, clean-shaven) with his own dark hair tied back, no wig, in a dark wool coat, a plain waistcoat and riding boots, leaning forward on a brown horse at a gallop along a dirt road between a stone wall and a farmhouse, turning his head with his mouth open, calling out toward the farmhouse at the right, where in one lit window halfway up the picture a farmer in a nightshirt leans out holding a candle. The window is in the middle of the picture's height, well below the top right corner. A bright moon, nearly full, low over bare spring trees in the middle of the sky, not in a corner. The horse is much bigger than the man: its back is as high as a standing man's chest, and Revere sits small on it, his feet in stirrups; it has four legs in a true gallop. Seen from the roadside, a little below, Revere's head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, the window and the moon in the upper half. Only two people. No lantern in a church tower in the picture, no modern road. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. cards.fact: When her brother Ban Gu died with his history of the Han dynasty unfinished, the emperor had her complete it. She taught the empress and the ladies of the palace, and scholars came to her to learn to read the history.
cards.art: Ban Zhao about 106 in a room of the Han palace at Luoyang, teaching: a dignified Chinese woman of about sixty with gray hair pinned up under a simple dark headdress, in a long layered silk robe of dark red and black with wide sleeves, kneeling at a low lacquered table and pointing with a brush to a column on an unrolled bundle of bamboo strips, while two young women of the court, each different in age and dress, kneel across the table and follow her brush. All three wear Han dynasty dress as the tomb figurines and paintings of the period show it: a long robe wrapped round the body with a crossed collar, plain or with a small woven pattern, long wide sleeves, a narrow sash; the young women's hair gathered in a low knot at the nape of the neck. No kimono, no wide obi sash, no floral prints, no dangling hairpins. Painted wooden pillars, a folding screen, a bronze lamp. Seen from across the table, Ban Zhao's head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, her brush and the strips in the upper half. Only three people. The marks on the strips cannot be read. No paper books, no later dynasties' dress, no fans or parasols. cards.fact: In 921 he set out from Baghdad as secretary of the caliph's embassy to the king of the Volga Bulgars, almost a year's journey. His account describes the Rus traders he met there, and a chieftain's funeral in a burning ship.
cards.art: Ibn Fadlan in 922 on the bank of the Volga, writing: an Arab scholar of about forty with a black beard, a white turban and a long traveling coat lined with fur, sitting on a folded rug on the riverbank with a writing case on his knee, his reed pen raised as he looks up from the page at what he sees. Beyond him on the wide gray river lie two wooden trading boats drawn up on the shore, and one Rus trader, a tall man with a short beard and a cloak pinned at the shoulder, unloads a bundle of furs. Birch woods on the far bank, a cold pale sky. Seen from behind his shoulder and to one side, his face turned so we see it, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, the river and the boats in the upper half. cards.fact: Army surgeons used to wait behind the lines until a battle was over. Larrey's flying ambulances, light carts on springs, went out under fire to bring the wounded in at once, and he treated wounded enemies like his own men.
cards.art: Dominique-Jean Larrey about 1797 on a battlefield in Italy, bringing in the wounded: a French army surgeon of thirty with long dark hair, a lean, determined face and no wig, in a dark blue coat with a high collar, kneeling on the ground beside a wounded young soldier in a white uniform of the other side, tying a bandage round his arm. Behind them stands a light, closed two-wheeled box carriage on leather and iron springs, painted dark green, pulled by two horses, its rear door folded down over a mattress floor, and one orderly in a plain coat helps a second wounded man up into it. Smoke drifts over a far hillside. Seen from low beside the wounded soldier, Larrey's head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, his hands tying the bandage in the upper half too; the carriage stands to one side behind him, its roof a sixth of the way down, not in a corner. Only four people. No red cross anywhere, no modern stretcher, no blood pools. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners.
